newsitem.title: FRANCE: Cr Lyonnais will need more state money to be sold.
newsitem.headline: Cr Lyonnais will need more state money to be sold.

text.p: Credit Lyonnais chairman Jean Peyrelevade said on Thursday that the state- controlled bank would need a fresh injection of public money before it can be privatised.

He made the comment after the bank reported a first-half profit of 67 million francs compared with a 36 million profit for the year earlier period. The profit was achieved after the state gave the bank 3.9 billion francs in emergency aid to remove the burden of costs imposed under last year's rescue.
He said the government would be unable to sell the bank in its current state as its solvency ratios were too low.
He said buyers would be unwilling to acquire the bank with its current Cooke ratio of 4.5 percent as it would mean a deterioration of their own solvency ratios.
The 4.5 Cooke ratio "permits us to live...with our current shareholder (the state)," Peyrelevade told a news conference.

"But (it) would be unbearable for whatever private shareholder...because none of our partners, French or European, would accept through a minority or majority stake in Lyonnais to take the risk of a deterioration of its own rating. That means that, if people want rapid (privatisation), it would need a recapitalisation (by the state)."

He said buyers would be unwilling to acquire the bank with its current solvency ratio as it would mean a deterioration of their own solvency ratios. He estimated that to improve the bank's Cooke ratio by one percentage point would require seven to eight billion francs in additional funds.

The Conservative government of Prime Minister Alain Juppe announced last week that it wanted to privatise the bank as soon as possible and said it would mount another bailout -- the third in three years -- to ready it for sale.
Sources have said Credit Lyonnais is unlikely to be ready until early 1998.

Finance Minister Jean Arthuis said at last week's announcement that the government would wait until the release of the half year figures to say how much might be needed to get the bank ready for sale. But press reports have forecast the government will have to inject at least 10 billion francs into the bank to boost its balance sheet.
Peyrelevade said the bank would prepare a privatisation plan by the year-end.

He also said that, to privatise the bank, the government would also have to address the concerns of ratings agencies whose confidence in the bank rests partly on the state's presence as majority shareholder.
"We are at the limit (with our rating) that allows us to operate in the markets," and obtain good results, he said.
The bank is currently rated BBB+ by U.S. ratings agency Standard & Poor's.
